newsitem.title: USA: Another study finds abortion-cancer link.
newsitem.headline: Another study finds abortion-cancer link.

text.p: Another study has found that abortion may slightly raise a woman's risk of getting breast cancer but the same researchers pointed out a flaw that could skew the results of these controversial studies.

The research, which suggested that women were not accurately reporting their abortion history, appeared in Wednesday's edition of the Journal of the National Cancer Institute and was released Tuesday.
Several recent studies have found a slightly elevated link between abortion and breast cancer and they have been seized on by anti-abortion advocates.

The latest epidemiology study, by Matti Rookus and Flora van Leeuwen at the Netherlands Cancer Institute in Amsterdam, compared 918 breast cancer patients and an equal number of healthy women. All the women had given birth at least once.

The women were interviewed about their reproductive history, including abortions. The team found that the cancer patients reported a higher rate of abortions. But by comparing that "self-reported" data to some independent health records on contraception, the team found that the self-reported data on abortion might not be reliable.

In a conservative part of the Netherlands, where abortion is less acceptable, the abortion-cancer link was much higher than in other regions. That led the researchers to test the women's reports of birth control use with actual prescription records, and they found bigger gaps in accuracy in the conservative region, leading them to suspect that similar accuracy problems marred the abortion data.

In an accompanying editorial, Dr. Douglas Weed and Dr. Barnett Kramer of the U.S. National Cancer Institute said the study made a "creative and fortuitous" contribution to understanding reporting bias.
"For very personal and perhaps even subconscious reasons, women -- especially healthy women -- underreport this emotionally laden decision," they wrote.
